Yellow Face from the Suffering of the People

"Feeling the Sorrow of Others" in a Tale by Saadi

In his tale of the Damascus famine, Saadi speaks of a man who is not himself in financial hardship, yet the suffering of the hungry robs him of pleasure. Can one, in times of war, economic hardship, and insecurity, be concerned about the suffering of others and still carry on with life?

In this episode, inspired by Saadi's tale, we explore the meaning of empathy in hard times; we speak about the necessity of compassion and of lessening the suffering of others, and we reflect on how the flood of images of suffering on social media can gradually desensitize us. In this installment, we will also seek answers to these questions: Is happiness in times of hardship a sign of indifference, and how can discontent become a criterion for judging others?

Taqi Pournamdarian is a literary scholar, a prominent researcher of Persian literature, and a professor at the University of Tehran, who has devoted an important part of his scholarly life to the study of mystical poetry and the thought of Iranian mystics. He is considered one of the leading figures in the study of mysticism and literary criticism in contemporary Iran, and his research on Rumi, Hafez, and the symbolic language of mystical texts holds a special place in literary studies. Among his well-known works are "Ramz va Dastan-haye Ramzi dar Adab-e Farsi" (Symbol and Symbolic Tales in Persian Literature), "Didari ba Simorgh" (A Visit with the Simorgh), and "Gomshode-ye Lab-e Darya" (The Lost One at the Edge of the Sea). Death of Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh; Professor and Researcher of Political Geography and Geopolitics of Iran

Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh, professor and researcher of political geography and geopolitics of Iran, passed away in the early hours of today in London.

Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh, a political geographer and renowned Iranian researcher, was one of the figures who devoted an important part of his scholarly and research work to Iran's political geography, border issues, the Persian Gulf, and Iran's geopolitical position in the region. His name is linked to discussions concerning Iran's territorial integrity, the three islands, and the strategic importance of the Persian Gulf.

Throughout his scholarly career, Mojtahedzadeh contributed to discussions on political geography and Iran's national interests through authoring books and publishing articles and specialized viewpoints — a field in which knowledge of history, geography, and power relations is of fundamental importance for understanding Iran's position in the region. He was among the researchers who spent their lives studying Iran's land, history, and political situation. May his memory be cherished, and may his loss be condoled to his family, friends, academic colleagues, and the scholarly community of Iran.

@sahandiranmehr

The historical instance of this view can also be found in history. In Book Five of the History of the Peloponnesian War, written by Thucydides, the dialogue between the Melians and the Athenians is detailed.

The story was that in 416 BC, Athens asked the small island of Melos to surrender to its empire. The Melians tried to maintain their neutrality and hoped that justice, independence, and the possibility of help from Sparta would protect them, but the Athenians stated their argument clearly:

"The issue is not only our present enemies; independent islands like you are also a danger to the empire, because they stand outside our order... if peoples maintain their independence, it is because they have power; and if we do not attack them, it is because we fear them. So by subjugating you, in addition to expanding our empire, we also increase our security; especially since you are islanders and weaker than others and should not be able to prevail over the masters of the sea."

(Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book Five, Section 97)

The cycle of violence and a tale from Kalila wa Dimna
Violence does not end when the fighting stops; rather, its effects sometimes begin at the very moment it is thought to be over.
In this episode, we turn to the story of a bird that, after years of soaring free and companionship in the court of power, falls victim to violence and is caught in its trap.
This tale from Kalila wa Dimna is not merely about revenge; it is a narrative about trust, power, violence, and the collapse of a relationship, raising these questions: What makes one side's violence permissible and the other side's violence a crime?
